extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, mathematicians, and students of physics (readers of Newton's Principia)
extracted.subtask_description: Foundational methodological rules and core definitions from Newton's Philosophiae Naturalis Principia (preface and early definitions): how to conduct natural philosophy (science) and precise definitions of mass, motion, forces, absolute/relative time/space/motion, and related quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical method: follow phenomena and real causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Ad veram philosophiam pertinet, rerum naturas ex causis vere existentibus derivare: eas vero leges quaerere, quibus voluit summus opifex hunc mundi pulcherrimum ordinem stabilire; non eas quibus potuit, si ita visum fuisset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer theories that derive the natures of things from actually existing causes and seek the laws that (it is presumed) the Supreme Designer chose to establish the world's order, rather than inventing hypotheses of what could have been. Follow causes as evidenced by phenomena (experiments and observations) rather than fictitious or yet-unproven suppositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses must be shown to exist or be refuted
rubrics_metrics.description: If phenomena can be explained by hypotheses, one has not yet given true philosophy unless those hypotheses are shown to exist or at least shown not to exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing unobserved entities (e.g., subtle media, vortices, atmospheres), the proposer must either demonstrate their real existence or demonstrate that they do not exist; otherwise the explanation remains mere fiction and unworthy of true philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of causes (parsimony requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Omnis enim causa debet esse effectu suo simplicior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causes invoked to explain phenomena ought to be simpler than the effects they explain. Avoid unnecessarily complex or compounded hypotheses when simpler, adequate explanations are available. Example: fictitious vortices that more complexly account for planetary motion are inferior to simpler hypotheses that match observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy must be founded on experiments and observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Sana omnis & vera philosophia fundatur in phaenomenis rerum: ... non ab incertis conjecturis petere, sed observando atque experiendo addiscere debemus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True natural philosophy is based on phenomena; laws and principles should be learned from observation and experiment rather than uncertain conjecture. The editor praises experimental demonstration (e.g., pendulum experiments, observations of comet and planetary motions) as primary evidence for physical principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting speculative media absent demonstrable efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Qui caelos materia fluida repletos esse volunt, hanc vero non inertem esse statuunt; hi verbis tollunt vacuum, reponunt. ... ex cometarum phaenomenis, nullam esse hujus aetheris efficaciam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume the existence or dynamical efficacy of hypothetical subtle fluids (aethers) unless observations demonstrate such efficacy. For example, cometary motions provide evidence against an aether that would exert appreciable resistive or driving effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition I — Quantity of matter (mass)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitas materiae est mensura ejusdem orta ex illius densitate et magnitudine conjunctim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass is measured by the conjunction of density and magnitude; practical recognition of this quantity is via weight (ponderi proportionalem esse reperi per experimenta pendulorum). Notes include how density multiplies with compression (e.g., air doubled in density in doubled space gives quadruple quantity in same space).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition II — Quantity of motion (momentum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitas motus est mensura ejusdem orta ex velocitate et quantitate materiae conjunctim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The quantity of motion of a body is the product of its mass and its velocity; the total motion equals the sum of the motions of the parts. Examples: a body twice as massive with same velocity has twice the motion; doubling velocity quadruples motion (in combined-mass examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition III — Vis insita (innate force / inertia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Materiae vis insita est potentia resistendi, qua corpus unumquodque, quanticum in se est, perseverat in statu suo vel quiescendi vel movendi uniformiter in directum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vis insita (vis inertiae) is the power of matter to resist change of state (to preserve rest or uniform linear motion). It is proportional to the body (mass) and manifests only when another force acts. Distinguishes between resistance (resistentia) and impetus related to interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition IV — Vis impressa (impressed force)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vis impressa est actio in corpus exercita, ad mutandum ejus statum vel quiescendi vel movendi uniformiter in directum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An impressed force is an action applied to a body to change its state; it acts during action but does not persist afterward. Examples: impact, pressure, centripetal action are forms of vis impressa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition V — Vis centripeta (centripetal force)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vis centripeta est, qua corpora versus punctum aliquod, tamquam ad centrum, undique trahuntur, impelluntur, vel utcunque tendunt. Hujus generis est gravitas, vis magnetica, & vis qua planetae retrahuntur a motibus rectilineis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centripetal force is any force that draws bodies toward a point (center), e.g., gravity or magnetism; it is what causes curvature of motion and retention in orbits. If such a force were absent, projectiles would move in straight lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition VI — Vis centripeta (absolute quantity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vis centripeta quantitas absoluta est mensura ejusdem major vel minor pro efficacia causae eam propagantis a centro per regiones in circuitu.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The absolute quantity of a centripetal force measures its total efficacy as propagated from the center through regions of the surrounding medium or field; examples include magnetic strength varying with magnet size or intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition VII — Vis centripeta acceleratrix (accelerative quantity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vis centripeta quantitas acceleratrix est ipsius mensura velocitati proportionalis, quam dato tempore generat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The accelerative measure of centripetal force is the acceleration it produces (velocity generated in a given time). Examples: magnetic or gravitational accelerating effect differs with distance (greater near, lesser far). This quantity yields how bodies accelerate under the centripetal cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition VIII — Vis centripeta motrix (motive quantity / weight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vis centripeta quantitas motrix est ipsius mensura proportionalis motui, quem dato tempore generat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The motive quantity corresponds to the effective 'weight' or total centripetal propensity of the whole body toward the center (proportional to its mass and to the accelerative force). Near Earth's surface, motive force (weight) is proportionate to the product of mass and local accelerative gravity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology caution: mathematical usage vs physical mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Porro attractiones & impulsus eodem sensu acceleratrices & motrices nomino. ... Caveat lector, ne per hujusmodi voces cogitet me speciem vel modum actionis causamve aIicubi definire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton warns that words like attraction, impulse, propensity are used mathematically to denote quantities, not to assert a physical mode or mechanism of action. Readers should not infer that 'centers' literally have physical forces unless so demonstrated; mathematicians treat these concepts abstractly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute vs relative time (Scholium I)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tempus absolutum, verum, & mathematicum, in se & natura sua sine relatione ad externum quodvis, aequabiliter fluit; Relativum, apparens, & vulgare est sensibils & externa quaevis durationis per motum mensura.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish absolute (true, mathematical) time, which flows uniformly in itself, from relative (apparent) time measured by motions (hours, days). Astronomical corrections (equation of time) and experiments (oscillatory clocks, eclipses of Jupiter's satellites) are necessary to relate apparent measures to absolute time; absolute time itself cannot be altered though measured durations may vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute vs relative space (Scholium II)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spatium absolutum, natura sua sine relatione ad externum quodvis, semper manet similare & immobile; Relativum est spatii mensura seu dimensio quaelibet mobilis, quae a sensibus nostris per situm suum ad corpora definitur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute space exists independently and remains similar and immobile; relative space is the measure or dimension we take with respect to bodies (e.g., space defined by land, air, or celestial relation to Earth). Movements measured relative to other bodies may hide absolute change; one must be careful when inferring absolute rest from relative measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place / locus definition (Scholium III)
rubrics_metrics.description: Locus est pars spatii quam corpus occupat, estque pro ratione spatii vel absolutus vel relativus. Pars, inquam, spatii; non situs corporis vel superficies ambiens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place (locus) is the part of space occupied by a body; it is properly a part of space (absolute or relative), not merely the body's surface or situation. The total motion equals the sum of motions of parts; locus of whole equals sum of loci of parts—this underpins conserved quantities and reasoning about motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute vs relative motion (Scholium IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Motus absolutus est translatio corporis de loco absoluto in locum absolutum; relativus de relativo in relativum. Quies relativa permansio corporis in eadem navis regione; quies vera permansio in eadem parte spatii illius immoti.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute motion is translation with respect to absolute space; relative motion is with respect to relative measures (e.g., a ship's hold). Examples: a person appearing at rest inside a moving ship is relatively at rest but absolutely moving with the ship. Absolute motions combine contributions from Earth's motion, ship's motion, and the person's motion within the ship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experiments to correct apparent measures (e.g., equation of time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tempus absolutum a relativo distinguitur in Astronomia per aequationem temporis vulgi. ... Hujus autem aequationis in determinandis phaenomenis necessitas, tum per experimentum horologii oscillatorii, tum etiam per eclipses satellitum Jovis evincitur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Astronomical phenomena require correcting apparent (vulgar) time measurements via equations derived from observation and experiment. Examples include using pendulum clocks and eclipses of Jupiter's moons to detect inequalities in apparent time and relate them to absolute time for accurate celestial measurements.
